text: We have a network of n nodes. You get a list called times, where each entry u, v, w means a signal goes from u to v and takes w time. A signal starts at node k. Return the time for all nodes to get it, or minus one if some node never does.
Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. The edges are directed, right? A signal on u, v, w only goes from u to v, not back.

Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a node gets the signal at the earliest time it can be reached from k. So its arrival time is the shortest path from k to that node. And all nodes have the signal when the last one gets it. So the answer is the max, over all nodes, of the shortest distance from k. If even one node is unreachable, that max is infinity, so I return minus one. Are there any constraints on the input size? And can weights be negative?
n is up to a hundred, and weights are zero to a hundred — never negative.

Good — non-negative weights is the key fact. It means I can use Dijkstra. Let me run through the example: edges two to one, two to three, and three to four, each costing one, with k equal to two. Node two is at time zero, nodes one and three at time one, and node four at time two. The last one is node four at time two, so the answer is two. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every path from k and keep the shortest to each node. That blows up — too many paths. This problem reminds me of a classic single-source shortest path. Because all weights are non-negative, Dijkstra is the right tool. Bellman-Ford would also work, but it's V times E — slower here for no reason. So: run Dijkstra from k, get the shortest distance to every node, then take the max.

Here's the plan. One: a dist array, infinity everywhere except zero at k, and a min-heap of distance, node pairs. Two: pop the closest pair; skip it if it's stale, otherwise lock in its distance and relax its out-edges. Three: return the largest distance, or minus one if any node is still infinity. One thing worth flagging: I don't decrease keys. When I find a shorter path to v, I push a new pair and leave the old one in the heap. The guard, if d is greater than dist of u, continue, throws those stale pairs away when they surface — that's lazy deletion. It keeps the code simple without hurting the complexity: at most one push per successful relax, so pushes stay order E. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I build an adjacency list of size n plus one, since nodes are numbered from one, and a dist array full of INT MAX. I push zero, k, then pop the smallest pair, skip it if it's stale, and push a new distance whenever a relax improves. At the end, any node still at INT MAX means minus one; otherwise I return the max. One thing worth flagging: the heap uses greater of P, so it's a min-heap — priority queue is a max-heap by default. And the pair is distance, node, not node, distance, so it sorts by distance. Get either wrong and the whole thing breaks.

Let's dry-run the code with an example: five nodes, k equals one, seven edges — expected six. The row that matters is the pop of five, three. That pair is a leftover: node three was first reached at cost five straight from node one, but going through node two later found it at cost three. When the old pair pops, five is bigger than dist of three, which is three, so I skip it. Final distances are zero, two, three, five, six, so the answer is six — node five hears the signal last. That matches. Corner cases: one edge from one to two with weight one, and k equal to one, gives one. The same graph with k equal to two gives minus one, since node one is unreachable. A zero-weight edge is fine — that node just gets the signal at time zero.

The time complexity is E log V. Each edge causes at most one push, so the heap holds order E pairs, and each pop or push is a log of that. The space complexity is V plus E — the adjacency list, the dist array, and the heap. In the worst-case scenario, a dense graph has about V squared edges, so it's about V squared log V. With n at most a hundred, that's tiny. Oh, one more thing — the stale guard is not required for a correct answer. The relax check, d plus w less than dist of v, already blocks useless updates. But without the guard, I'd expand already-settled nodes again and waste time. So it's an efficiency guard, not a correctness one.

Nice. Three things stood out. You reframed everyone got the signal as the max of the shortest paths right away. You pinned the correctness of Dijkstra on the non-negative weights. And you explained lazy deletion clearly — why the stale guard is about speed, not correctness, and why total pushes stay order E. Well done.
